topicAssessments.reasoning: Temperature is related to mean random translational kinetic energy in the classical equilibrium ideal-gas model and gas-rest frame, not bulk-flow kinetic energy or all molecular energy. This supplies the conditions absent from the source's brief introductory statement.

One-mole normalization, molar volume, number density and the Avogadro reference are retained. Native (3-11) uses n as number density. With molar V_mu in volume/mol, nV_mu and N_A both have inverse-mole units; multiplying density by an actual sample volume gives its particle count. The text explicitly invokes the book's molar notation rather than substituting an arbitrary sample volume or dimensionless count into the equation. Avogadro's source scientific naming identity is declared; no new historical claim.

Multiplying p=(2/3)n times mean E by molar volume gives (3-12). Equating it with (3-13) for the same equilibrium ideal gas gives (3-14) by dividing by (2/3)N_A. Dimensional check: pV_mu, N_A times mean E and RT all have energy/mol units; R/N_A has energy/kelvin units and (3-14) gives energy per molecule. Absolute temperature in kelvin is required, not Celsius. Mean E is center-of-mass translational kinetic energy, excluding rotation, internal vibration and interaction potential energy. All original formulas and section references remain literal.

Proportionality refers to absolute temperature and mean translational energy. For the same molecular mass, mean E=m times mean squared speed/2 makes the squared-speed mean increase with temperature. It does not require identical individual speeds or equal average speeds between different gases at the same temperature.

The source's extension to other phases and gas/wall comparison is retained but requires classical equipartition and comparable kinetic degrees of freedom; Newtonian dynamics alone is not sufficient. Classical independent quadratic momentum terms have equal temperature-dependent mean contributions, whereas interaction energy can differ. Crystal vibrations are distinguished from liquid motion; liquids are not universally assigned lattice sites. Equal kinetic means under the stated conditions do not imply equal total microscopic energy.

The preceding zero-temperature trend is explicitly a classical extrapolation. The source-linked footnote qualifies low-temperature failure of the approximation and identifies a minimum-energy quantum state, not cessation of all motion. Bound particles may retain zero-point motion; no universal claim that every system's entire kinetic energy vanishes is made.
